To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GABAA receptor coupling junction and pore mutations cause gain or loss of function, which is likely linked to early-onset epileptiform encephalopathies.

the GABRB3 missense mutations identified in patients with EOEE and profound developmental delay cause functional defects in GABRB3 that affect GABAA receptors and are linked to the clinical phenotype.

the three GABRB3 mutations (L170R, A305V, and T288N) are associated with EOEE and profound developmental delay, and the mutations cause gain of function, loss of function, and differential sensitivity to the GABAA agonist diazepam, which are associated with the GABA binding and gating coupling junction and channel pore.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that cause epilepsy, and how they can be exploited for the development of novel antiepileptic drugs.
the identification and characterisation of GABAA receptor mutations that cause EOEE.
the molecular mechanisms of GABAergic neurotransmission and how defects in GABAR function and biogenesis can cause early-onset epilepsies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GABAA receptor coupling junction and pore mutations are linked to EOEE.
GABRB3 missense mutations in EOEE patients can affect the receptor function by either causing gain of function or loss of function, depending on the location of the mutation.
GABRB3 mutations that alter GABAA receptor coupling junction and/or pore residues cause EOEE.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the three de novo mutations in GABRB3 that we have studied are all in the extracellular domains and are all in regions that are involved in receptor activation.
the GABAergic system is a promising target for EOEE and that the GABRB3 gene is a promising candidate gene for EOEE.

mutations in the GABA binding site (L170R), the coupling junction (A305V), and the channel pore region (T288N) are linked to EOEE, and that these mutations cause gain of function (L170R, A305V) and loss of function (T288N).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the molecular mechanisms by which GABAA receptor mutations cause EOEE can be complex and multifaceted and that they can affect the biophysical function of the receptor and/or its biogenesis.
the molecular mechanisms of EOEE are likely to be complex, involving multiple sites of action in the GABAB3 subunit, and may be linked to altered GABAergic signalling and synaptic transmission.
mutations that affect the GABAA channel gating machinery can cause severe epilepsy and that this can be linked to the specific molecular mechanisms by which the mutation affects receptor function.
